quiz.q: An error handler has On Error Propagate type=ANY first, then HTTP:NOT_FOUND, then MULE:EXPRESSION. A MULE:EXPRESSION error occurs. Which handler runs?
quiz.explain: Handlers are checked in order and the first match wins. ANY matches every error, so placed first it catches the MULE:EXPRESSION error — which is why ANY must always be last.

quiz.q: A flow has handlers for HTTP:NOT_FOUND, MULE:EXPRESSION and ANY (last). A wrong weather host causes HTTP:CONNECTIVITY. Where does it go?
options: Mule's default error handler, because no specific handler exists
quiz.explain: No specific handler matches HTTP:CONNECTIVITY, so the catch-all ANY handler takes it. Without ANY it would have gone to the default error handler.

quiz.q: The ANY handler is changed to On Error Continue and its Transform Message sets statusCode = 500. A connectivity error occurs. What does the client receive?
options: No response — the request times out
quiz.explain: On Error Continue sends a success to the next level, so the Listener's success Response section is used (200 by default). That section does not use the error status variables.

quiz.q: A child flow called via Flow Reference raises an error and has no matching handler. What happens?
options: The error propagates to the parent flow's error handler
The child flow retries the failed component
quiz.explain: If the child has no matching handler, the error propagates to the parent; if the parent's handler matches, it executes and the Listener returns its Error Response.

quiz.q: You add an error mapping on an HTTP Request: HTTP:CONNECTIVITY → WEATHER:CONNECTIVITY. An existing handler is typed HTTP:CONNECTIVITY. What happens on a connectivity failure?
options: The HTTP:CONNECTIVITY handler no longer matches; a handler must use WEATHER:CONNECTIVITY
Both types are raised, so both handlers run
Error mapping only changes the description, not the type
quiz.explain: After mapping, the error object carries WEATHER:CONNECTIVITY, so handlers must match the new type. In the demo it fell through to ANY.

quiz.q: How do you make one named Error Handler apply to every flow in the application?
options: Copy it into each flow's error-handling section
Global Elements → Configuration → set Default Error Handler to the named handler
Name it 'default' in the Error Handler properties
quiz.explain: Create a named Error Handler in a separate Mule configuration file and set it as Default Error Handler in a Configuration global element (or reference it per flow).

quiz.q: Why can't you drag On Error Propagate directly onto the canvas of a new common-error-handler.xml file?
options: It must be inside an Error Handler component
It must be inside a Try scope
Global files only accept On Error Continue
quiz.explain: On Error Propagate can't be dropped at top level; you first drag an Error Handler (a box/scope) and put the handlers inside it.

quiz.q: You want an HTTP Request and a Transform Message to fail without stopping the rest of the flow. Which approach matches the class?
options: Wrap them in a Try scope with On Error Continue
Add an ANY On Error Propagate at flow level
Use a Choice router with a Default route
quiz.explain: Try gives component-level error handling. With On Error Continue inside, the error is handled in Try and processing continues after it.

quiz.q: A loan applicant's age is 67. Nothing technically failed, but the business rule says reject. Which component raises this error?
quiz.explain: Technical errors are raised automatically; business errors are raised with Raise Error using your own namespace:identifier type and a description.

quiz.q: The Raise Error type is set to BUSINESS:<identifier>. In this type, what is BUSINESS?
quiz.explain: The type format is namespace:identifier — the namespace is the main category (BUSINESS) and the identifier is the specific error.

quiz.q: A Choice router has route 1 (age 18–29), route 2 (age 30–40), route 3 (age 41–65) and Default. The request has age 35. What runs?
quiz.explain: Choice evaluates routes in order and runs only the first one whose condition is true; later routes are skipped.

quiz.q: You paste copied components into a new handler and Studio asks about duplicate doc IDs. What should you do?
options: Click No to keep the same IDs
quiz.explain: Every component has a unique doc ID in the XML; clicking Yes regenerates the duplicates.

cards.back: Matches all errors. Use it as a catch-all handler and always place it **last**.
Right-click a component → **Go to XML** to jump to its XML. Used to copy components without "Copy of" names.
An empty handler is a self-closing tag. Drag a dummy Logger in to get opening/closing tags, paste between them, then delete the dummy.
The unique ID of each component in the XML. When pasting duplicates, accept Studio's offer to regenerate them.
The parent is the calling flow; the child is the flow called via **Flow Reference**.

cards.front: On Error Propagate vs On Error Continue?
cards.back: Propagate handles the error and re-throws it to the next level (Listener Error Response). Continue handles it and returns **success** (Listener Response, 200 by default).
Handlers are evaluated in order and the first match wins. ANY matches everything, so specific handlers after it are never reached.

cards.front: Child flow error — where is it handled?
cards.back: In the child's matching handler (then propagated up); if none matches, in the parent's handler; ultimately the Listener's Error Response.

cards.front: How often is On Error Continue used?
cards.back: Roughly 10–25% of the time, mainly with the **Try** scope (e.g. inside For Each or Scatter-Gather). On Error Propagate is used most of the time.

A connector-operation setting that converts its error type into a custom one, e.g. `HTTP:CONNECTIVITY` → `WEATHER:CONNECTIVITY`. Handlers must then match the new type. Rare in practice, but asked in certification.
**Flow** level (flow's error section), **application/global** level (named Error Handler), **component** level (Try scope).
A container of On Error Continue/Propagate handlers; routes an error to the **first matching** handler. Can be named and global.
Set in Global Elements → Configuration (`defaultErrorHandler-ref`). Applies a named Error Handler to all flows in the app.
If flow A calls flow B via Flow Reference, A's handler also applies to errors propagated from B. Independent flows don't share flow-level handlers.
Component-level error handling for one or a group of components. Create via select → right-click → **Wrap in → Try**.

cards.front: Empty On Error Continue inside Try
cards.back: Allowed — it just swallows the error and the flow continues.
Raises a custom (business) error with type `NAMESPACE:IDENTIFIER` and a description, e.g. age not within limits.

cards.front: Raise Error with no error handler — response?
cards.back: Goes to the default handler: in the demo, **500 Server Error** with the description as the body.
Conditional routing like if / else if / else. Routes evaluated in order, **first match** runs, **Default** runs if none match.
On Error Propagate, On Error Continue, Raise Error, Error Handler, Try scope.

cards.front: App won't start because of a port
cards.back: Another app was still running in Studio. Stop it first (Debug mode also uses port 6666).

cards.front: Status for unknown errors in the ANY handler
cards.back: Keep **500 Internal Server Error**, since unknown errors are usually server-side.
